objectives: Distinguish bit depth from sample rate.

slides.title: Sampling: continuous → discrete time
slides.body:
Digital audio is discrete samples of a continuous waveform.

**Sample rate** $f_s$: samples per second (Hz). Common rates:
- **44.1 kHz**: CD audio. Captures up to 22.05 kHz (above audible range for most adults).
- **48 kHz**: video / pro audio standard.
- **96 kHz**: high-end pro audio.
- **192 kHz**: niche; extreme audiophile.
- **8 kHz**: telephony (captures up to 4 kHz, speech-intelligible).
- **44.1 / 48 kHz × 2 (88.2, 96) or × 4 (176.4, 192)**: integer multiples.

**Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem**: a signal band-limited below $f_s/2$ can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples at rate $f_s$.
$$f_{\text{max}} < f_s/2 \quad \text{(Nyquist frequency)}$$

Intuition: at sample rate $f_s$, the highest representable frequency has two samples per cycle (one peak, one trough). At lower sampling, the same waveform would be ambiguous.

**Aliasing**: if input contains frequencies ABOVE $f_s/2$, they 'fold back' into the audible range as false frequencies. A 30 kHz tone sampled at 44.1 kHz appears as $44.1 - 30 = 14.1$ kHz — wrong frequency, audible artifact.

**Anti-aliasing filter**: a low-pass filter before sampling, removing frequencies above $f_s/2$. Mandatory in ADCs. Modern designs use steep-cutoff digital filters (linear-phase IIR, polyphase).

**Reconstruction**: from samples back to continuous waveform. Theoretically: convolve with sinc function. In practice: DACs use multistage interpolation + low-pass filtering.

**Why 44.1 + 48 kHz**: 44.1 = Sony's pick (related to NTSC video framerate × 3-line audio sampling). 48 = pro / video standard. Above 22 kHz isn't necessary for audibility; higher rates help in mixing (anti-aliasing margin, transient processing) but inaudible directly.

slides.title: Bit depth + dynamic range
slides.body:
**Bit depth**: bits per sample. Determines dynamic range + noise floor.

Common:
- **16-bit**: CD audio, consumer files. 65,536 quantization levels.
- **24-bit**: pro recording + mixing. 16.7 million levels.
- **32-bit float**: pro mixing in DAWs. Effectively infinite dynamic range.

**Dynamic range** = ratio between loudest + quietest representable sample. For $n$-bit linear PCM:
$$\text{DR} \approx 6.02 n + 1.76 \,\text{dB}$$
- 16-bit: ~96 dB.
- 24-bit: ~144 dB.
- 32-bit float: ~1500 dB theoretical (way beyond any analog system).

**Why higher bit depth in mixing**:
- Many tracks summed amplifies quantization noise.
- Effects (especially nonlinear: compression, distortion) magnify noise.
- Bit-depth headroom prevents accumulated error from being audible.
- 32-bit float: no clipping in intermediate processing.

**Final master is usually 16/24-bit**: reduce from 32-bit float at master step, with **dithering**.

**Quantization noise**: error between true sample value + nearest quantization level. Approximately uniform [-q/2, +q/2] where q is the LSB step. For high-amplitude signals, sounds like white noise. For low-amplitude signals (~1 LSB), looks like a distorted version of the signal — correlated, audible as gritty distortion.

**Dithering**: add small random noise BEFORE quantization. Decorrelates quantization error → sounds like benign noise. Critical when converting from 24-bit → 16-bit (the final mastering step).

**Dither types**:
- TPDF (triangular probability density function): standard, doesn't add a DC component.
- Noise-shaped dither: moves the dither noise to less-audible frequencies (high frequencies; ear less sensitive). MORE listener-friendly. Many mastering plugins offer.

**Audible difference between 16-bit + 24-bit dithered**: blind tests show most listeners CAN'T reliably distinguish (Meyer + Moran 2007). Higher bit depths matter in production; for finished masters, 16/24-bit is adequate.

slides.title: Aliasing + the digital domain pitfalls
slides.body:
Aliasing isn't just an input issue. INSIDE the digital domain, processing can create new frequencies above the Nyquist limit, which then alias.

**Nonlinear processing aliasing**:
- Distortion / saturation: creates harmonics. A 5 kHz sine through hard clipping creates 15, 25, 35, ... kHz overtones. At 44.1 kHz sampling: 25 kHz → aliases to 19.1 kHz. 35 kHz → 9.1 kHz. Audible as a 'cheap digital' sound.
- Compression: less aliasing because compression is roughly linear at most levels.
- Synthesis: digital oscillators producing rich waveforms (square, saw, FM) generate harmonics that alias.

**Solutions**:
- **Oversampling**: process at 2× or 4× the sample rate, then anti-alias filter + decimate back. Standard for distortion/saturation plugins. CPU cost: 2-4× more.
- **Band-limited synthesis**: synthesize waveforms with harmonics explicitly limited to <Nyquist. Wavetables, additive synthesis, BLEP/PolyBLEP techniques.
- **Higher sample rates**: working at 96 kHz pushes Nyquist to 48 kHz, leaving headroom for harmonics before aliasing.

**Listening for aliasing**: rough, gritty, 'digital' artifact. Cleanly-tuned harmonics shouldn't alias; if you hear non-harmonic 'sparkle' or buzzy artifacts, suspect aliasing.

**Sample-rate conversion**: changing between 44.1 + 48 kHz isn't trivial. Naive methods cause aliasing or alias-image artifacts. Quality conversion uses polyphase filters or sinc interpolation. Tools: SoX, Resampler, Voxengo r8brain.

**Jitter**: timing inaccuracy in the sample clock. Causes phase noise; audible artifacts in very-low-jitter systems. Modern interfaces have <100 picoseconds jitter; most production setups have negligible issues.

**Latency** in digital audio:
- ADC + DAC: ~2-5 ms each.
- Plugins: depends; many introduce buffering (a few ms to 100s of ms).
- Round-trip recording latency: typically 5-20 ms. Higher latencies feel disconnected when playing instruments.
- USB / FireWire / Thunderbolt audio interfaces optimized for low latency.

question.question: Apply Nyquist to a specific signal
question.goal: Microphone captures audio with frequencies up to 18 kHz. What minimum sample rate to avoid aliasing? (Plus practical considerations.)

steps.prompt: In practice, anti-aliasing filters aren't infinitely steep. They roll off over a transition band. So real systems use sample rates somewhat higher than 2× the max signal. Common choices for 18 kHz?

options: 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz — gives ~3-6 kHz transition band for the anti-alias filter to roll off cleanly without affecting the audible signal.

steps.reveal: 44.1 or 48 kHz. Provides margin for the anti-alias filter to roll off without affecting audible content.

steps.prompt: Why is 44.1 kHz used for CD audio specifically?

options: Historical: derived from PCM-encoded audio on PAL/NTSC video formats. 44.1 = 245×60×3 ≈ 44,100 — fit the available bits in video.

steps.reveal: Historical: PCM video standards yielded ~44 kHz. Sony picked 44.1 for Compact Disc in 1980. 48 kHz came later for digital video synchronization. Both are now standard — DAWs handle either + conversion when needed.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Nyquist: } f_s > 2 f_{\text{max}}, \text{ practically with margin}}$$ All digital audio respects Nyquist; the only question is how much margin + filter slope. 44.1 / 48 kHz cover audible range comfortably. 96 / 192 kHz exist for production headroom (anti-alias margin, transient response, pitch-shifting headroom) — not for direct listening, where they're inaudibly different from 48 kHz.

question.question: When converting a 24-bit master to 16-bit CD format, why is dithering recommended?
options: Quantization error in the truncation step is signal-correlated (creates audible 'gritty' distortion at low levels). Adding small random noise (dither) before truncating decorrelates the error → sounds like benign hiss instead. Critical for low-level signals (fades, reverb tails).
question.explanation: Without dither, truncating bit depth produces signal-correlated quantization noise → audible distortion especially at low signal levels (the noise becomes a distorted version of the signal). Dither adds uncorrelated noise that masks the distortion. Result: noise floor sounds like white/pink hiss, which is far less objectionable than rough distortion. TPDF (triangular) dither is industry standard for 24→16 conversion. Noise-shaped dither pushes noise to less-audible HF region. Always dither when reducing bit depth.

slides.workedSolution: Truncation: signal-correlated quantization error. At low levels = audible gritty distortion. Dither: small uncorrelated noise (~1 LSB amplitude) added before truncating. Decorrelates the error → sounds like benign hiss, perceptually masked by the music. Critical step in mastering for final delivery formats (CD 16-bit, streaming 16-bit). Modern noise-shaped dither concentrates noise above 10 kHz (less audible).

question.question: Diagnose a distorted digital recording
question.prompt: A live recording sampled at 44.1 kHz has strange high-pitched whistles + 'sizzle' on cymbals. Walk through whether this could be aliasing + what to do.
Explain in two or three sentences why higher sample rates (96 kHz, 192 kHz) are used in production but typically NOT audible in finished masters.
question.rubric: Mentions that higher rates give the anti-alias filter more headroom + allow nonlinear processing (saturation, FM) to produce harmonics without aliasing; in production, the math is cleaner; for direct listening, content above 22 kHz is inaudible to humans. Blind tests consistently fail to distinguish 48 vs 96 kHz when end-listener delivery is the same. Production-tier convenience, not audible difference.
